1.pericope_label: Paul, called to be an apostle of Jesus Christ through the will of God, and Sosthenes our brother, unto the church of God which is at Corinth, to them that are sanctified in Christ Jesus, called to be saints, with all that in every place call upon the name of Jesus Christ our Lord, both theirs and ours: grace be unto you, and peace, from God our Father, and from the Lord Jesus Christ

schools.summary: Gill explains that the writer is named Paul though his Jewish name was Saul, and that a Jew born in a Roman city might well carry two names, going by the one among the Jews and by the other among the Gentiles; he notes that Paul presses his office because some in the church, through the insinuations of the false apostles, demurred at it. To be called the church of God he calls a very high character, a number of persons gathered out of the world and joined in holy fellowship, and observes that it is given here to a people among whom were many irregularities, errors, disorders and divisions, which shows that a church of God is not to be unchurched for everything amiss in it. Calvin observes that Paul proceeds this way in almost all his introductions, securing authority to his doctrine from the station assigned him by God and favour from his affection to those he writes to, since we believe much more readily a man we look upon as regarding us with affection. On the title of the church he states the difficulty at its full strength — that it may appear strange to give the name to a multitude infested with so many distempers that Satan might be said to reign among them rather than God — and answers from the Lord’s promise that he had much people in that place, and from the tokens of a true Church still remaining among them: the doctrine of the gospel, baptism, and the Lord’s Supper. He warns that we may not require the Church while in this world to be free from every wrinkle and stain, nor pronounce unworthy of the title every society in which everything is not as we would wish, since the man prepossessed with the notion that there is no Church where perfect purity is not seen must in the end withdraw from all others and look upon himself as the only saint in the world, or set up a peculiar sect in company with a few hypocrites. On the greeting he refers the reader to his commentary on Romans, not willingly burdening him with repetitions.

Henry treats the opening as the preface to the whole epistle, noting that the church at Corinth was one Paul himself had planted though there were some among them who now questioned his apostleship and vilified his person and ministry — the most faithful and useful ministers not being secure from such contempt. He observes that Paul had not taken the honour to himself but had a divine commission, that asserting the character was proper at any time but necessary at this time when false teachers made a merit of running him down and their deluded followers set them up in competition with him, and that maintaining his apostolical character in that juncture was not pride but faithfulness to his trust; the joining of a minister of lower rank with himself he reads as part of the same modesty. John Lightfoot documents the double name as a national custom: among Jews a Jewish name and among heathens another, either the same name turned into the heathen language — Tabitha and Dorcas, Thomas and Didymus — or a different name altogether, as Herod in the one place is Agrippa in the other and John is also Mark, and he cites a gloss that Israelites outside the land of Israel have names like the names of the Gentiles. On the description of the readers he takes the phrase to be set against those sanctified in the law, and derives the title of saints from the Septuagint’s rendering of a holy convocation, where the feasts and the sabbath are called holy to the Lord; sanctified in Christ he treats as a general word subdivided into those who are truly saints and those who, calling on the name of the Lord, are saints by profession.

Clarke opens with an account of Corinth — its situation on the isthmus between two ports, its command of the navigation and commerce of the Ionian and Aegean seas, its destruction by the Romans and its opulence — before coming to the verse, where he reports the proposal of Bishop Pearce that a comma be placed after the participle so that the phrase reads Paul the called, the apostle of Jesus Christ, the first word signifying being called to and the other sent from; the participle he takes as possibly meaning constituted, and observes that since the apostle had many irregularities to reprehend it was necessary he should be explicit in stating his authority, deriving no part of it from man. Sanctified he glosses as separated from the corruptions of their place and age, and the title of saints as constituted saints or invited to become such, that being the design of the gospel. The address to all in every place he takes as showing the apostle intended this epistle to be the general property of the universal Church, though several matters in it are suited to the state of the Corinthians only, and the closing words as declaring Christ the common Lord and Saviour of all, the exclusive property of no one church or people. Wesley finds great propriety in every clause, particularly this one, since some at Corinth called the authority of his mission in question, and observes that by the mention of God the authority of man is excluded and by the mention of the will of God the merit of Paul; the naming of the companion he reads as both humility and prudence in an epistle wherein so many irregularities were to be reproved, and the word brother as emphatical, of one who from a Jewish opposer of the gospel became a faithful brother. He notes that the plain appellation used here is the one Paul reserves for the churches he addresses familiarly, that the good wishes for every true Christian upon earth suit the catholic love the epistle labours to promote, and that calling upon the name plainly implies that all Christians pray to Christ as well as to the Father through him.

Barnes devotes the whole of his first block and half of his second to an introduction — the situation of Corinth and the character of its inhabitants, the establishment of the church, the time and place of writing, the occasion, and the divisions of the epistle — before reaching the verses. On the commission he refers the will of God to the special revelation granted at the conversion, notes how often Paul insists he did not act on his own authority, and explains the emphasis here by the fact that his apostolic authority had been called in question at Corinth. Of the companion he records that he is named as the chief ruler of the synagogue, beaten before the judgment-seat, and that it is evident he was not then a Christian; when he was converted, or why he had left Corinth and was now with Paul, is unknown, and he was neither an apostle nor is there reason to think him inspired — but Paul used an amanuensis, often associated others with himself, and would find it conciliating to name a man so well known at Corinth. He observes that the title church of God is applied without hesitation to a body among whom great disorders had been introduced; that sanctified does not refer to the profession of holiness but implies they were in fact holy and separated from the mass of heathens; and that called does not refer merely to an external invitation but to that which was made effectual. The address to all in every place he takes as evidence that Paul expected the epistle to be read beyond Corinth, and calling upon the name as implying worship and proving the Lord Jesus an object of it. Ellicott renders the opening as a called Apostle, the authority being set out at the commencement because it was questioned by some in Corinth, and conjectures from the joined name that the companion was the amanuensis, only the closing salutation being written by Paul’s own hand. He credits Chrysostom with the remark that the opening words are a protest against the party-spirit prevailing there — the Church of God, not of this or that man — treats those sanctified not as another class of persons but as a description of the whole, and insists that the term saints is never used by Paul with its restricted modern meaning but applied to the whole baptised Church, the nearest English word being Christians in its most comprehensive sense. Robertson takes the opening as a verbal adjective without the verb to be, so literally a called apostle, not so-called but one whose apostleship is due neither to himself nor to men but to the will of God, and notes that though Paul knows he is not one of the twelve he is on a par with them because chosen by God, the refusal of the Judaizers to recognise him making him the more careful to claim his position. The genitive in the address he takes to show the church belongs to God and not to any individual or faction, and he sets the description against the city itself, destroyed and restored a century apart and now very rich and very corrupt, its name having become a verb for practising vile immoralities in the worship of Aphrodite.

Chrysostom sees Paul casting down their pride from the very first word, since what he learnt he did not discover of himself nor acquire by his own wisdom, but was called while he was persecuting and laying waste the Church; of him that calleth is everything and of him that is called nothing, so to speak, but only to obey. He turns the naming of Christ against them — your teacher is Christ, and do you register the names of men as patrons of your doctrine? — and reads the will of God as excluding worth in the called, since it was because it seemed good to him that they were called and not because they were worthy; the joining of a lesser name he takes as another instance of modesty, Paul stationing with himself one far beneath him. Cyril of Jerusalem, on the sanctifying, argues that since man is of twofold nature, soul and body, the purification also is twofold, the one incorporeal for the incorporeal part and the other bodily for the body: the water cleanses the body and the Spirit seals the soul, so that one going down into the water should not think of the bare element but look for salvation by the power of the Holy Ghost, since without both no man can possibly be made perfect.

Tertullian treats the superscription as a standing form recurring in every epistle, and fixes on the fact that what the apostle prescribes for those he writes to is not the usual health but grace and peace. He declines to ask what a destroyer of Judaism has to do with a formula the Jews still use, since to this day they salute each other with the greeting of peace and formerly did so in their Scriptures, and takes the practice as corroborating the Creator’s own declaration about the beauty of the feet of those who preach the gospel of peace: the herald of good, that is of God’s grace, was well aware that peace was to be proclaimed along with it. He adds that in announcing these blessings as from God the Father and the Lord Jesus the apostle uses titles common to both.

debates: Whether sanctified describes fact or profession: Barnes denies it refers to profession and holds they were in fact holy, while John Lightfoot subdivides the general phrase into those truly saints and those saints by profession, and Ellicott declines the distinction altogether by applying the term to the whole baptised Church.

On what ground a body so disordered may be called the church of God: Gill answers that a church is not to be unchurched for everything amiss in it, Calvin grounds it in the surviving tokens of gospel doctrine, baptism and the Supper together with the promise given at Corinth, while Robertson and Ellicott make the phrase a matter of the genitive and a protest against party spirit rather than a verdict on the members.
outliers: Clarke reports a proposal to repunctuate the opening, placing a comma after the participle so that Paul is called the called, and the title of apostle stands separately — the first word signifying being called to and the second being sent from.

Calvin turns the title of the church into a warning against purism, holding that whoever requires a spotless Church must end by withdrawing from everyone and reckoning himself the only saint in the world, or founding a sect of his own with a few hypocrites.

Chrysostom makes the single word called a rebuke of Corinthian pride before any argument has begun, on the ground that everything belongs to the one who calls and nothing to the one called but obedience.

4.pericope_label: I thank my God always on your behalf, for the grace of God which is given you by Jesus Christ; that in every thing ye are enriched by him, in all utterance, and in all knowledge; even as the testimony of Christ was confirmed in you

schools.summary: Gill introduces the passage as a thanksgiving for various blessings bestowed on the church, a proof of the apostle’s great affection and of how much its welfare lay at his heart; God is styled his God to distinguish him from others, to express his faith of interest in him, and to observe to the church that all the good things they enjoyed came from him who was his God and their God, his Father and their Father. Being enriched he expounds as being plentifully provided by Christ with all grace and all the riches of grace, with his own unsearchable riches and with the riches of glory to which they were entitled, all of which come to them through his poverty, which makes the grace in the donation the more illustrious. The testimony of Christ he takes to be the gospel, which bears witness to his deity, incarnation, obedience, sufferings, death, resurrection, ascension and intercession, to redemption by his blood and justification by his righteousness; and its confirmation among them he attributes at once to the signs and miracles that attended the preaching, to the extraordinary gifts of the Spirit and particularly prophecy bestowed on many of them, and to the internal power and energy of the Spirit accompanying and applying it. Calvin explains the design: having secured authority for himself in the salutation from the station assigned him, he now endeavours to procure favour for his doctrine by expressing his affection, soothing their minds beforehand that they may listen patiently to his reproofs, and he quotes Theodoret giving the same view — that being about to censure them he soothes the organ of hearing beforehand, so that the remedy may be the more favourably received. On the confirming he reports that Erasmus rendered it the other way, that by these things the testimony of Christ was confirmed in them, but holds that the words convey another meaning and are easy if not wrested: God has sealed the truth of his gospel among the Corinthians for the purpose of confirming it. He observes that this might be done in two ways, either by miracles or by the inward testimony of the Holy Spirit, notes that Chrysostom seems to understand it of miracles, and takes it himself in a larger sense, since the gospel is properly confirmed in our experience by faith, it being only when we receive it by faith that we set to our seal that God is true.

John Lightfoot glosses the pair of gifts as the gift of tongues and prophesying, and identifies these with what the next verse calls the testimony of Christ — the testimony whereby Jesus is proved to be the true Messiah, seeing that he bestowed such gifts; he compares the saying that the testimony of Jesus is the spirit of prophecy, taking it to mean not only the doctrine the prophet uttered but the very gift of prophesying, and the three earthly witnesses, where the spirit is the gift of prophecy, the water baptism, and the blood martyrdom.

Clarke takes the grace given not only as their calling to be saints and to be sanctified in Christ Jesus but as the various spiritual gifts specified in the verses following, and insists that the word rendered utterance should certainly be translated doctrine and so understood: all the truths of God relative to their salvation had been explicitly declared to them, and they had all knowledge, so that they perfectly comprehended the doctrines they had heard. The testimony of Christ he takes as the gospel the apostle had preached, confirmed by the various gifts of the Holy Spirit and by the miracles the apostle wrought. Wesley glosses the constancy of the thanksgiving as meaning whenever he mentions them to God in prayer, keeps the utterance and knowledge to divine things, and observes that these were the gifts the Corinthians particularly admired, so that the congratulation naturally tended to soften their spirits and make way for the reproofs which follow; on the confirming he notes that they knew they had received these gifts by the hand of Paul, and that this consideration was highly proper to revive in them their former reverence and affection for their spiritual father.

Barnes observes that no small part of the epistle is occupied with reproofs, but that before proceeding to the specific statement of the disorders the apostle commends them for the attainments they had really made, showing he was disposed to concede all he could; it was no part of Paul’s disposition to withhold commendation where it was due, and a willingness to commend those who do well is as much in accordance with the gospel as a disposition to reprove where it is deserved, so that a minister, or a parent, may frequently do as decided good by judicious commendation as by reproof. Being enriched he takes to denote both that the blessings were conferred abundantly and that they were of inestimable value, properly called a treasure. On the confirming he holds that the gospel was at first established among them by the miraculous endowments of the Holy Ghost and that the same endowments were still continued, furnishing evidence of the divine favour in the same measure as when the gospel was first preached, the power to speak with tongues being a continued miracle; the testimony of Christ he calls the gospel, so named because it bears witness to Christ. Ellicott treats the thanksgiving as serving to secure at the very outset the attention of those written to, showing that the apostle is not blind to or forgetful of their good qualities although the epistle is specially written to rebuke their present sins, and that he is not about to utter words of hopeless condemnation but of wholesome warning; the emphatic singular, against the plural of the previous verses, he takes to indicate that Paul does not join his companion as author of the epistle but writes in his own name and with his sole authority. He renders the grace as given in Christ Jesus rather than by him, that is, given to them as being in Christ; he makes utterance the power of outward expression of the knowledge that dwells within; and he takes the testimony as that which Paul bore to Christ and from Christ, confirmed among them by the full bestowal of spiritual gifts. Robertson notes the singular verb of thanksgiving here and in two other letters against the plural in others, remarks that the grounds of Paul’s thanksgivings in his epistles are worthy of study, and observes that even in the church at Corinth he finds something to thank God for, whereas the second epistle has no expression of thanksgiving because of the acute crisis and neither has Galatians — here Paul allows his general attitude to override the specific causes of irritation. He points out in detail that the unusual spiritual gifts were the Corinthians’ glory and became their peril, glosses the verb for enriching as an old causative common in Attic writers which dropped out for centuries, reappeared in the Septuagint and is used in the New Testament by Paul alone, and calls the finding of real riches in Christ one of Paul’s pregnant phrases full of the truest mysticism. The genitive in the testimony he calls objective, the testimony concerning Christ and the witness of Paul’s preaching, and the verb for confirming he derives from a root meaning to make to stand, the special gifts having been given for that very purpose.

Chrysostom observes that what Paul exhorts others to do, in bidding them make their requests known with thanksgiving, he practises himself, teaching us to begin always from these words and before all things to give thanks; nothing is so acceptable to God as that men should be thankful, both for themselves and for others, and he prefaces almost every epistle so. The occasion here he finds more urgent than elsewhere, because he that gives thanks does so both as being well off and in acknowledgment of a favour — and a favour is not a debt, nor a requital, nor a payment, a thing important everywhere but much more among men who were gaping after the dividers of the Church. On the possessive he notes that out of great affection Paul seizes on what is common and makes it his own.

debates: What the Corinthians were enriched in: Clarke insists the first word means doctrine, so that the content of the gospel had been fully declared and comprehended; Ellicott makes it not content but faculty, the power of outward expression of an inward knowledge; John Lightfoot identifies the pair with tongues and prophesying, and Robertson with the unusual spiritual gifts that became their peril.

By what means the testimony was confirmed: Calvin reports that Chrysostom seems to understand it of miracles and himself takes it more largely of the inward testimony of the Spirit, since the gospel is properly confirmed in our experience by faith; Barnes and Robertson keep it to the miraculous gifts, while Gill declines to choose and lists miracles, gifts and inward energy together.
outliers: Barnes turns the verse into a rule of pastoral method, holding that a minister or a parent may frequently do as decided good by judicious commendation as by reproof.

Robertson observes which letters have no thanksgiving at all — the second epistle to this same church, because of the acute crisis, and Galatians — and reads the presence of one here as Paul letting his general attitude override his specific irritation.
Calvin quotes Theodoret in Greek for the tactical reading of the thanksgiving, that one about to censure first soothes the organ of hearing so the remedy may be received.

7.pericope_label: So that ye come behind in no gift; waiting for the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ: who shall also confirm you unto the end, that ye may be blameless in the day of our Lord Jesus Christ. God is faithful, by whom ye were called unto the fellowship of his Son Jesus Christ our Lord

schools.summary: Gill takes the gifts as ordinary or extraordinary alike, and observes that by the detail given later it appears they were not inferior in gifts to any of the churches. On the confirming he argues carefully that the author of the blessing is not Christ, though Christ is mentioned immediately before and seems to be the antecedent of the relative: the confirmation is made in Christ, and its end is that the saints should be blameless in the day of Christ, so the confirmer must be another, namely God the Father, to whom the apostle has been giving thanks and continues to give thanks through this verse. The assurance he grounds on the faithfulness of God, who is always true to his promises and will never suffer his faithfulness to fail, and on effectual calling, since whom he effectually calls by his grace he also glorifies. Calvin explains that when Scripture speaks of God as faithful the meaning in many cases is that in God there is steadfastness and evenness of tenor, so that what he begins he carries through to the end; the sense here is that God is steadfast in what he purposes, and consequently does not make sport as to his calling but will unceasingly take care of his work — the calling of each of his own is not mere play, and in calling them he does not mock them. On the verb of the first clause he supplies the philology: it means to be in want of what one would otherwise stand in need of, its proper sense being to come too late for a thing and so to miss it, as Xenophon writes that Abrocomas came too late for the battle; the sense is that the Corinthians abound in all the gifts of God so as not to be in want of anything. On the relative he holds that it refers not to Christ but to God, though God is the remoter antecedent, since the apostle is going on with his congratulation and now lets them know what hope he has of them as to the future, partly to assure them further of his affection and partly to exhort them by his own example to cherish the same hope.

Clarke takes every gift and grace of God’s Spirit to have been possessed by the members of that church, some having their gifts after this manner and others after that. On the waiting he raises the difficulty that it is hard to say whether the apostle means the final judgment or the Lord’s coming to destroy Jerusalem and make an end of the Jewish polity, and since Paul does not explain himself particularly he must refer to a subject with which the readers were well acquainted; he inclines to the judgment on the Jewish nation, and at the next verse sets the two readings expressly side by side, the day when Christ comes to judge the world according to some and the day when he comes to destroy the Jewish polity according to others, adding that while God destroys the disobedient he can save those who believe. The confirming he makes answerable to their conduct: as the testimony of Christ was confirmed among them, so in conscientiously believing and obeying, God will confirm them through that testimony. On the faithfulness of God he reports that the expression was a favourite one among the ancient Jews, who properly understood by it the integrity of God in preserving whatever is entrusted to him, and that they supposed human fidelity might illustrate the divine; he relates their story of Rabbi Phineas, with whom two men left two measures of barley and then forgot them, who each year for seven years sowed, reaped, threshed and stored the crop, and on their return bade them come and take their treasure. Wesley glosses the waiting as with earnest desire, and makes the posture diagnostic — a sure mark of a true or a false Christian, to long for or to dread this revelation. On the confirming he inserts a condition into the promise, who will also confirm you if you faithfully apply to him, and distinguishes the times: now it is our day, wherein we are to work out our salvation, and then it will be eminently the day of Christ and of his glory in the saints. The faithfulness of God he refers to all his promises, so that to him that hath shall be given, and the calling he takes as a pledge of God’s willingness to save to the uttermost.

Barnes glosses the verb as meaning they were not wanting or deficient, a word usually applied to destitution or poverty, and insists that the word for gift does not refer necessarily to extraordinary and miraculous endowments but includes also all the kindnesses of God towards them in producing peace of mind, constancy and humility, so that they possessed in rich abundance all the endowments bestowed on Christians. The confirming he takes as establishing them in the hopes of the gospel and making them firm amidst all their trials and all the efforts that might be made to shake their faith, keeping them to the end of life in the path of holiness; the sense, he says, is that they should be kept and should not be suffered to fall away and perish, and he calls it one of the many places which express the strong confidence of Paul that those who are true Christians shall be preserved. The evidence of that perseverance he rests on the fidelity of God, who is true and constant and will adhere to his promises, who will not promise and then fail to perform nor commence anything he will not perfect and finish. Ellicott corrects the English of the first clause, which is not that they come behind in no gift absolutely but that the result is their coming behind others in no gift, and takes the gifts as those which sustain them and enable them to wait for the revelation — the second visible appearance, which the early Church expected would soon occur — not with fear or with impatience but with a calm trustfulness. On the relative he considers the argument that the use of the full name for the day, instead of the possessive, shows the antecedent is not Christ, allows that this by itself would scarcely be sufficient since there are examples elsewhere of Paul using the name where a possessive pronoun would have seemed more natural, and decides from the general sense of the passage and especially of the following verse that the antecedent is God; he also distinguishes three distinct periods referred to in these verses. Robertson analyses the first clause as consecutive, with the infinitive and a double negative, and glosses the verb as meaning to be late; he calls the record here a wonderful one, but observes that in the second epistle Paul will have to complain that they had not paid their pledges for the collection made over a year before, a very modern complaint. The double compound for waiting he calls late and rare outside of Paul, an eager expectancy of the second coming; the relative pointing to Christ, in his reading; and the closing verbal adjective he renders unimpeachable, since none will have the right to impeach. On the faithfulness he notes it is the ground of Paul’s confidence, which he loves to state, and that God is both the agent of their call and the ground or reason for it; the word for fellowship he traces from partner through partnership and participation to intimacy, and to the sense of contribution, calling it high fellowship with Christ both here and hereafter.

Cyril of Jerusalem uses the verse to instruct candidates for baptism, showing how great a dignity the Lord bestows in transferring them from the order of Catechumens to that of the Faithful: since God himself is called Faithful, as he is called Good and Just and Almighty and Maker of the Universe, the one who receives that title in receiving the name receives a great dignity, and should consider to what a height he is rising in becoming partaker of a title of God.

debates: What the gifts are: Barnes denies the word refers necessarily to miraculous endowments and includes under it peace of mind, constancy and humility, while Robertson takes them as the unusual spiritual gifts and Gill declines to distinguish, allowing ordinary and extraordinary alike.

Which day is waited for: Clarke alone raises the possibility that the coming meant is the destruction of Jerusalem and the end of the Jewish polity rather than the final judgment, and sets the two readings side by side twice without deciding; Ellicott, Robertson and Wesley all take it as the second visible appearance without hesitation.

Who shall confirm them to the end: Robertson says the relative points to Christ, while Calvin, Gill and Ellicott all refer it past the nearer name to God — Gill because the confirmation is made in Christ and aims at blamelessness in his day, Ellicott from the general sense of the passage rather than from the wording of the phrase for the day.

Whether the keeping is unconditional: Barnes reads it as evidence that true Christians shall be preserved and not suffered to fall away, whereas Clarke makes the confirming answerable to conscientious believing and obeying, and Wesley writes the condition into the promise itself.
outliers: Robertson sets the commendation against the later record, noting that the church which came behind in no gift had still not paid its pledges to the collection a year after making them, and calls it a very modern complaint.

Clarke illustrates the faithfulness of God from a rabbinic tale of a man who for seven years sowed and reaped barley left with him and forgotten, then returned the whole increase to its owners as their treasure.
Cyril of Jerusalem reads the divine title as one the baptised come to share, so that being called faithful is itself a promotion into a name of God.

10.pericope_label: Now I beseech you, brethren, by the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, that ye all speak the same thing, and that there be no divisions among you; but that ye be perfectly joined together in the same mind and in the same judgment. For it hath been declared unto me of you, my brethren, by them which are of the house of Chloe, that there are contentions among you. Now this I say, that every one of you saith, I am of Paul; and I of Apollos; and I of Cephas; and I of Christ

schools.summary: Gill observes that the apostle, having taken notice of the many favours bestowed on the church, now turns to the divisions fomented in it, and that he does not use his apostolical power and authority nor lay his injunctions and commands upon them, which he might have done, but most affectionately beseeches them, styling them brethren as being children of the same Father, members of the same body and partakers of the same grace — a reason why they should not fall out by the way. He notes that the report was no groundless suspicion or jealousy of the apostle’s but a matter laid wholly open to him, the proof so strong and the evidence so full that they could not deny it, and that the charge that every one of them said this is not to be pressed of every individual member but of many, and the far greater number, who were in these factions. Calvin explains the change of tone: hitherto he has handled them mildly, knowing they were much too sensitive, but now, having prepared their minds for correction, he acts the part of a good and skilful surgeon, who soothes the wound when about to apply a painful remedy, and begins to handle them with more severity — though even here with great moderation. The sum, he says, is that the Lord has not in vain conferred so many gifts upon them, and they must take heed lest graces so distinguished be polluted by their vices. Naming the informants he explains by the rule that general observations usually have little effect, so that the application is designed to make them perceive it was not without good reason that harmony was urged: they had not merely turned aside from the holy unity which ought to be among Christians but had fallen into contentions, which are much more dangerous than jarring. On the watchwords he mentions the figure by which a writer repeats his opponents’ own expressions, prefers to read the particle as a conjunction giving the reason for the previous statement, and answers the objection that no contention yet appears by saying that where there are jarrings in religion men’s minds will soon afterwards burst forth into open strife.

Henry says the apostle here enters on his subject, exhorting them to unity and brotherly love and reproving their divisions; he had received an account from some who wished them well, prompted neither by ill-will to the church nor to their ministers but by a kind and prudent concern to have these heats qualified by Paul’s interposition. He paraphrases the appeal as urging them, if they have any regard to that dear and worthy name by which they are called, to be unanimous and to avoid all alienation of affection from each other, and qualifies the demand twice — that in the great things of religion they be of a mind, and that they be joined together as far as they can. John Lightfoot addresses the last watchword from the Jewish side and offers two accounts of it: if there were any among the Corinthians who had been baptized with the baptism of John only, as there were among the Ephesians, it is no wonder they should say they were of the Messiah, not knowing as yet that Jesus of Nazareth was he; or, granting that all were better taught by Paul or Apollos, since very many still inclined to Judaism one may suspect they said it in the sense in which they had formerly been instructed concerning the Messiah, namely that every one should be enrolled and subjected under him only as Captain, and not under any deputed by him or supplying his place.

Clarke takes the apostle to have finished his introduction and to come now to his second point, exhorting them to abstain from dissensions; the appeal is by Christ’s authority and in his place, and on account of their infinite obligations to his mercy in calling them into such a state of salvation. On the demand that they speak the same thing he allows that if they did not agree exactly in opinion on every subject they might notwithstanding agree in the words they used to express their religious faith, and observes that on every essential doctrine of the gospel all genuine Christians agree, so that he asks why religious communion need be interrupted. The contentions he distinguishes from the divisions as the altercations these produced, since once divided they must necessarily contend in order to support their respective parties. Chloe he supposes some very religious matron at Corinth whose family were converted to the Lord, some of them probably sent to inform the apostle of the dissensions, and he conjectures that the three men named at the close of the epistle were her sons; he enumerates four sects — followers of Paul, of Apollos, of Cephas, and of Christ — and conjectures, following John Lightfoot, that the Gentile part of the converts boasted the names of Paul and Apollos and the Jewish those of Cephas and Christ, adding that these might again be subdivided, some preferring the apostle as the immediate instrument of their conversion and others Apollos for his extraordinary eloquence. Wesley reads the appeal as made by the endearing name of our Lord Jesus Christ, infinitely preferable to all the human names in which they gloried, glosses the schisms as no alienation of affection from each other and asks whether the word is ever taken in any other sense in Scripture, and divides the closing pair into the mind, meaning affections and desires, and the judgment, touching all the grand truths of the gospel. Chloe he has heard supposed the wife of Stephanas and the mother of Fortunatus and Achaicus, by which three the Corinthians had sent their letter to the apostle. Of the last party he says they spoke well, if they had not on that pretence despised their teachers, and wonders whether they valued themselves on having heard Christ preach in his own person.

Barnes marks this verse as the entry on the discussion of the irregularities at Corinth, the first being the divisions and strifes, and traces those divisions to the influence of philosophy, the ambition for distinction, and the exhibition of popular eloquence among the Corinthian teachers, which gives occasion for the discussion of wisdom that follows. He observes that the Corinthians had not informed him of their contentions in the letter they sent, so that he had heard of them incidentally, and takes the address to them as brethren for a token of affectionate regard even while administering a needed rebuke. Chloe he judges most probably a member of the church at Corinth, some of whose family had been at Ephesus while Paul was there. On the watchwords he reports that it has been doubted whether the parties had actually taken the names specified or whether Paul uses them as suppositions to show the absurdity of ranging themselves under different leaders, and that many of the ancient interpreters supposed he was unwilling to specify the real names. Ellicott introduces the party-spirit as one of the chief reasons for the writing of the epistle, and insists on a distinction: the factions rebuked were not sects who separated themselves from the Church but those who within the Church divided into parties, each calling itself by the name of some apostle whose teaching and practice were most highly esteemed. Of Chloe he says frankly that who she was we cannot tell, though her name was evidently well known to the Corinthians, and supposes some slaves of her household, probably travelling between Ephesus and Corinth on their owner’s business, brought the account of the distracted state of the church. On the last watchword he records the suggestion that it is not the designation of a fourth party but an affirmation by the apostle himself, in contradistinction to those who called themselves after the names of men, and rejects it both because there is no change in the form of expression to indicate a change of sense and because evident traces of the existence of such a party are found elsewhere. Robertson glosses the opening verb as an old and common word meaning to call to one’s side, corresponding to the verb of thanksgiving earlier and making this a direct appeal after the thanksgiving; the name he takes as genitive, the medium or instrument of the appeal rather than its cause, and the clause that follows as expressing purport rather than direct purpose. The demand that they all speak the same thing he identifies as an idiom from Greek political life, and this touch of the classical writers he takes to argue Paul’s acquaintance with Greek culture. Of the informants he notes that the words rendered as of the household are not in the Greek, though they correctly interpret it, and that whether these were the children, the kinspeople or the servants of Chloe we do not know, as it is likewise uncertain whether she lived in Corinth or in Ephesus, probably Ephesus. Of the party leaders he identifies the second as the eloquent Alexandrian whose philosophical and oratorical preaching contrasted with the studied plainness of Paul, remarks that people naturally have different tastes about styles of preaching and that this is well, and observes that Apollos himself refused to be a party to this strife, soon returned to Ephesus and refused to go back to Corinth; the third name he notes is the Aramaic one given Simon by Jesus, which Paul almost always uses.

Chrysostom reads the verse as an example of what he has continually been saying, that we must frame our rebukes gently and gradually. Being about to enter upon a subject full of many dangers and enough to tear up the Church from her foundations, Paul uses very mild language: his word is that he beseeches them, and beseeches them through Christ, as though not even he were sufficient alone to make this supplication and to prevail — meaning, Chrysostom says, that he takes Christ to fight on his side and to aid him, His injured and insulted Name, an awful way of speaking. The reason is that they should not prove hard and shameless, for sin makes men restless: if you sharply rebuke at once you make a man fierce and impudent, but if you put him to shame you bow down his neck, check his confidence, and make him hang down his head.

debates: Who Chloe was: Clarke makes her a religious matron of Corinth and the three men named at the close of the epistle her sons; Wesley reports her supposed the wife of one of them and mother of the other two; Ellicott says plainly that we cannot tell, and takes the messengers for slaves of her household; Robertson holds even their relation to her unknown and thinks she probably lived at Ephesus rather than Corinth.

Whether the four watchwords are the real party names: Barnes reports the old doubt, and that many ancient interpreters supposed Paul substituted his own name and his colleagues’ because he was unwilling to specify the actual leaders; Calvin mentions the figure by which a writer repeats his opponents’ own expressions.

What the last watchword means: Ellicott records and rejects the suggestion that it is not a fourth party but the apostle’s own counter-affirmation; John Lightfoot explains it either from a baptism that had not yet named Jesus as Messiah or from a Judaizing refusal to be enrolled under any deputy of the Messiah; Wesley grants that they spoke well, apart from the pretence.
outliers: Chrysostom turns the verse into a rule of reproof — sharp rebuke makes a man fierce and impudent, while shame bows down his neck and checks his confidence.
Robertson notes that Apollos, whose name was taken in vain in the quarrel, refused to be a party to it, returned to Ephesus, and would not go back to Corinth.
Wesley challenges the reader to find the word for schism used in any other sense in Scripture than alienation of affection.

13.pericope_label: Is Christ divided? was Paul crucified for you? or were ye baptized in the name of Paul? I thank God that I baptized none of you, but Crispus and Gaius; lest any should say that I had baptized in mine own name. And I baptized also the household of Stephanas: besides, I know not whether I baptized any other

schools.summary: Gill reports that some read the first clause as an assertion, that Christ is divided, his body the church being divided by such factions, while in some copies the note of interrogation is placed before it; he answers in the negative, since the human body was not to be divided, a bone of it not to be broken, the seamless garment not to be rent asunder, nor is the mystical body to be torn in pieces by schisms, nor is any one part of the gospel different from or opposite to another. On the thanksgiving he guards carefully: not that the apostle disliked the ordinance of baptism or the administration of it, much less thought it criminal or an evil in him to perform it, nor was he at any time displeased at the numbers who desired it of him, but on the contrary rejoiced when proper subjects were brought to submit to it; but since some in the church made an ill use of his having baptized them, he was greatly thankful it was so ordered. He notes the variant by which the fear is that they should say they were baptized in his name, and takes the reason to be lest any should reproach him as having drawn disciples to himself. Of the household he observes that the apostle, having said he baptized none but two, recollects himself and corrects it, thinks the head of that house the same man as the jailer baptized at Philippi, now removed to Corinth and become famous and useful there, and insists that no argument can be formed from the baptism of his household in favour of infant baptism. Calvin holds that Christ alone must reign in the Church, and that since the object of the gospel is that we be reconciled to God through him it is necessary first that we should all be bound together in him; because only a very few of the Corinthians, better advised than the others, retained Christ as their Master while all made it their boast that they were Christians, Christ was by this means torn asunder, for we must be one body if we would be kept together under one head. On the thanksgiving he says the words very sharply reprove the perversity of the Corinthians, which made it necessary for the apostle to avoid, in a manner, a thing so sacred and honourable as the administration of baptism; he would have acted with propriety and in accordance with the nature of his office had he baptized ever so many, but rejoices that it happened otherwise, and acknowledges it as ordered in the providence of God, that they might not take occasion from it to glory in him, nor he bear any resemblance to ambitious men who gather followers to themselves.

Henry gives the account of the apostle’s ministry among them and states the difficulty of the thanksgiving without evading it: how was this a proper matter for thankfulness? Was it not a part of the apostolical commission to baptize all nations? And could Paul give thanks to God for his own neglect of duty? He answers that Paul is not to be understood as if he were thankful for not having baptized at all, and lists those he did baptize — the former ruler of the synagogue at Corinth, Gaius, and the household of Stephanas, besides whom he did not remember having baptized any. John Lightfoot notes that the name of the first is also in use among the Talmudists, and builds an argument from the second: if that Gaius or Caius to whom the Third Epistle of John is written were the Corinthian Gaius, which he thinks very probable when the greeting in Romans is compared with that epistle, then John seems to have written his first epistle to the Corinthians, since he says he writes to the church, meaning certainly some particular church, and one where Gaius himself resided.

Clarke asks whether Christ can be split into different sects and parties, whether he has different and opposing systems, or whether the Messiah is to appear under different persons; on the second question he argues that since the gospel proclaims salvation through the crucified only, Paul has not poured out his blood as an atonement for them, so that being called by his name is absurd, and his disciples they should be alone who has bought them by his blood. To be baptized into the name of one, he explains, implied that the baptized was to be the disciple of him into whose name and religion he was baptized. He takes the apostle’s care not to baptize as care lest it should be supposed he wished to make a party for himself, since superficial observers might imagine he baptized them into his own name, though he baptized them into the name of Christ only, and he records the manuscript variation in the verb. Of the household he notes from the close of the epistle that they were the first converts in Achaia, probably converted and baptized by the apostle himself, and he reproduces at length John Lightfoot’s conjecture about Gaius and the Johannine epistles, crediting him by name. The closing admission that he does not recollect he defends warmly, protesting that it is strange the doubt expressed here should be construed so as to affect the apostle’s inspiration, and asking whether the inspiration of prophet or apostle necessarily implies perfect recollection of every circumstance. Wesley asks whether all the members are not still under one head, whether Christ alone was not crucified for them all and they all baptized in his name, and concludes that the glory of Christ is not to be divided between him and his servants, nor the unity of the body torn asunder, seeing Christ is one still; the fear he glosses as being lest any say he had baptized in his own name in order to attach them to himself, the thanksgiving as a pious phrase for the common one, I rejoice, and the closing words as meaning that it does not at present occur to his memory that he baptized any other.

Barnes takes the general argument to be that Christ alone ought to be regarded as their Head and Leader, his claims arising from his crucifixion and acknowledged by their baptism being so pre-eminent that they cannot be divided nor the honours due to him rendered to another, and asks with strong emphasis whether this single supreme Head of the church had become the head of different contending factions. The thanksgiving he explains by the fact that Paul had not given any occasion for the suspicion that he intended to set himself up as the leader of a sect or party, and he records the ancient reading by which the fear is that they should say they were baptized into his name. Of the household he says the family was among the first converts in Achaia and had shown great zeal in aiding Christians, that from the manner of mention its head probably did not reside at Corinth when he was baptized though he might have moved there afterwards, and that whether there were any infants in the family does not appear. Ellicott renders the first clause as an assertion — Christ, in the communion of the Church, is rent, torn in fragments by you — and explains that the mention of the sacred name as a party-cry makes the apostle burst into an impassioned exclamation, after which there is a momentary pause before he returns to those who bore his own name, the two streams of thought mingling and rushing together. The thanksgiving he paraphrases as gladness that it was not so, since had he baptized a great many some might have said he had originally created a party in his own name; the evident importance and position of the two he did baptize, and their being the first converts, may account for his having departed from his usual practice in their case. The mention of the household he calls evidently a subsequent correction, the apostle having forgotten them and been reminded possibly by the man writing from his dictation, who would naturally have known the fact, since that household were the firstfruits of Achaia and its head was at Ephesus with Paul when the letter was written. Robertson parses the first verb as a perfect passive — does Christ stand divided — holds it probable though not certain that the clause is interrogative like those following, records that Hofmann called the assertory form a rhetorical impossibility, and notes that the absence of the negative particle merely allows an affirmative answer which is true. The fourth party, he says, claimed to possess Christ in a sense not true of the others, and perhaps its leaders with their arrogant assumptions of superiority are the false apostles who pose as angels of light. He identifies the first man baptized as the ruler of the synagogue before his conversion, bearing a Roman cognomen, and the second by a Roman praenomen, probably the host of Paul and of the whole church and possibly though not clearly the hospitable Gaius of the third epistle of John, their prominence explaining why Paul baptized them. He recalls that Jesus himself baptized no one, to avoid this very kind of controversy, notes that some at Corinth were already laying emphasis on the person of the baptizer, and rejects the claim of those who would make Paul a sacramentalist; the household he calls an afterthought, and reports the suggestion that the amanuensis reminded him of the case.

Cyril of Jerusalem supplies the doctrine of baptism that stands behind the question: since man is of twofold nature, soul and body, the purification also is twofold, the one incorporeal for the incorporeal part and the other bodily for the body, so that the water cleanses the body while the Spirit seals the soul. One going down into the water should not think of the bare element but look for salvation by the power of the Holy Ghost, since neither he that is baptized with water but not found worthy of the Spirit, nor he that is virtuous in his deeds but does not receive the seal by water, receives the grace in perfection.

debates: Whether the opening clause is a question or a statement: Ellicott reads it as an assertion that Christ is being torn in fragments; Gill reports both readings, notes the manuscripts that punctuate it as a question, and answers it in the negative; Robertson thinks it probably interrogative while recording that Hofmann called the assertory form a rhetorical impossibility.

What the apostle is thankful for: Henry raises the objection that thanks for not baptizing looks like thanks for neglecting a commission, while Gill and Calvin both insist he would have acted rightly in baptizing any number and is thankful only for a providence that spared him the appearance of gathering a party.

Whether the baptizing of a household bears on infants: Gill denies flatly that any argument for infant baptism can be formed from it, while Barnes says only that whether there were any infants in the family does not appear.
outliers: John Lightfoot turns a name in this verse into an argument about the Johannine epistles, reasoning that if the Gaius of the Third Epistle is the Corinthian one, then the First Epistle of John was written to the Corinthians — a chain Clarke reproduces at length under his name.
Robertson recalls that Jesus baptized no one himself in order to avoid exactly this controversy, and uses the verse to deny that Paul can be claimed as a sacramentalist.

Clarke protests at interpreters who take the apostle’s admission that he does not recollect as a difficulty for his inspiration, asking whether inspiration must imply perfect recollection of every circumstance.

17.pericope_label: For Christ sent me not to baptize, but to preach the gospel: not with wisdom of words, lest the cross of Christ should be made of none effect

schools.summary: Gill notes that some think the apostle refers to his particular mission, in which no mention is made of administering baptism, but holds that he had no doubt the same commission the rest of the apostles had, which was to baptize as well as preach; indeed if he had not been sent at all to baptize it would have been unlawful for him to administer baptism to any person whatever. His sense, therefore, is that baptism was not the chief and principal business he was sent about, that work being done mostly by the preachers who travelled with him or followed after him. Calvin takes the clause as anticipating an objection that the apostle had not discharged his duty, since Christ commands his apostles to baptize as well as teach, and answers that this was not the principal department of his office, the duty of teaching having been principally enjoined upon him; when Christ gives the commission he connects baptism with teaching simply as an addition or appendage, so that teaching always holds the first place. Two things he insists must be noticed: that the apostle does not absolutely deny having a command to baptize, which belongs to all the apostles, since he would have acted rashly in baptizing even one person had he not been furnished with authority, but simply points out the chief thing in his calling; and that he does not by any means detract, as some think, from the dignity or utility of the sacrament, the question here being not the efficacy of baptism at all. The division of labour he explains by two considerations — that it was given to few to teach while many could baptize, and that many could be taught at the same time while baptism could only be administered to individuals successively, one by one — so that Paul, who excelled in the gift of teaching, applied himself to the work more especially needful for him and left to others what they could more conveniently accomplish.

Henry treats the verse as showing the manner in which Paul preached the gospel and the cross: not with the wisdom of words, the enticing words of man’s wisdom, the flourish of oratory or the accuracies of philosophical language upon which the Greeks so much prided themselves, and which seem to have been the peculiar recommendations of some of the heads of the faction in that church who most opposed the apostle. He preached otherwise lest the success should be ascribed to the force of art and not of truth, not to the plain doctrine of a crucified Jesus but to the powerful oratory of those who spread it, whereby the honour of the cross would be diminished or eclipsed. Paul, he observes, had been bred up himself in Jewish learning at the feet of Gamaliel, but in preaching the cross of Christ he laid his learning aside, preaching a crucified Jesus in plain language and telling the people that he who was crucified at Jerusalem was the Son of God and Saviour of men, and that all who would be saved must repent of their sins, believe in him, and submit to his government and laws. This truth needed no artificial dress but shone out with the greatest majesty in its own light, prevailing in the world by its divine authority and the demonstration of the Spirit without any human helps, so that the plain preaching of a crucified Jesus was more powerful than all the oratory and philosophy of the heathen world. John Lightfoot explains the apostle’s practice from the difference of the field: Paul was not appointed a baptist among the Gentiles as John was a baptist among the Jews, nor was the office of the one and the other alike. The Jews, even from their cradles, were instructed in the doctrine of the Messiah and in the articles of religion, so that John had no need to spend much pains preparing them for baptism in the name of the Messiah then to come and for the reception of the gospel; but the Gentiles had not so much as ever heard either of Christ or of the true God, so that Paul preached daily and, as it were, instilled the doctrine of religion into them drop by drop, it being no small labour leisurely to lead them to a baptizable measure.

Clarke reports and adopts Bishop Pearce’s translation, that Christ sent him not so much to baptize as to preach the gospel, and gives the reasoning behind it: the writers of the Old and New Testaments almost everywhere, agreeably to the Hebrew idiom, express a preference given to one thing beyond another by an affirmation of that which is preferred and a negation of that which is contrary to it, and so it must be understood here — for if Paul was not sent at all to baptize he baptized without a commission, whereas if he was sent to preach rather than baptize he discharged his duty aright. He adds that it appears sufficiently evident baptizing was considered an inferior office, though every minister of Christ might administer it. Wesley glosses the denial as meaning that baptism was not his chief errand and that those of inferior rank and abilities could do it, while noting that all the apostles were sent to baptize also; the wisdom of speech he explains as the artificial ornaments of discourse invented by human wisdom, and states the danger exactly — the whole effect of Paul’s preaching was owing to the power of God accompanying the plain declaration of the great truth that Christ bore our sins upon the cross, but this effect might have been imputed to another cause had he come with that wisdom of speech which the Corinthians admired.

Barnes takes the meaning to be that baptism was not the apostle’s main business, though he had a commission in common with others to administer the ordinance and occasionally did so, and observes that the same was true of the Saviour, who did not personally baptize. He offers reasons why the work was probably entrusted to ministers of inferior talents or to those permanently connected with the churches rather than to men travelling from place to place: first, the one the apostle suggests here, that had the apostles themselves baptized it might have given occasion to strifes and to the formation of parties, since those baptized by an apostle might claim some superiority over others; and second, that the rite was probably preceded or followed by a course of instruction adapted to it, which could be better entrusted to those who were to remain as ordinary religious teachers, it being an advantage that the same person should impart the instruction and administer the ordinance. Ellicott notes that preaching was eminently the work of the apostles and that the deacons used to baptize, and takes the mention of the preaching of the glad tidings as the apostle’s opportunity to state in vindication of himself why that, and not philosophy, was the subject of his preaching — adding that such, and not inability or ignorance, was the grand cause of his simplicity. Robertson locates the qualification in the syntax, the negative going not with the infinitive but with the verb of sending, so that Christ did not send him to be a baptizer, with linear action, as John the Baptist was; to be a gospelizer is Paul’s idea of his mission as Christ’s apostle, which led of course to baptism as a result, though Paul usually had it done by others, as at Caesarea the baptism was ordered done apparently by the brethren who were present. He notes Paul’s fondness for this late Greek verb and his occasional use of both verb and substantive together.

debates: Whether the denial is absolute: Clarke adopts a comparative rendering resting on a Hebrew idiom of preference, while Gill and Calvin reach the same result by argument — that the baptisms Paul did perform would otherwise have been unauthorised — and Robertson finds the qualification in the syntax, the negative attaching to the sending rather than to the infinitive.

Why baptizing was left to others: Barnes fears party feeling and points to the catechesis that accompanied the rite; Calvin argues from the scarcity of teachers and from the fact that many can be taught at once while baptism is administered one by one; Ellicott and Robertson simply record the practice; John Lightfoot grounds it instead in the difference between a Jewish and a Gentile mission field.
outliers: John Lightfoot contrasts the two baptizing offices by their audiences, holding that the Baptist inherited hearers catechised from the cradle while the apostle had to instil religion drop by drop into people who had never heard of the true God, and calls it no small labour to lead them leisurely to a baptizable measure.
Henry observes that Paul, trained in Jewish learning at the feet of Gamaliel, deliberately laid that learning aside when preaching the cross.
Calvin breaks off to insist that nothing in the verse detracts from the dignity or utility of the sacrament, the question here not being the efficacy of baptism at all.

18.pericope_label: For the preaching of the cross is to them that perish foolishness; but unto us which are saved it is the power of God. For it is written, I will destroy the wisdom of the wise, and will bring to nothing the understanding of the prudent

schools.summary: Gill distinguishes the subject from the Christian’s own cross, which he is to take up and bear for Christ’s sake — a doctrine taught by Christ and his apostles and found true by the saints in all ages, held in aversion and contempt as very disagreeable to the natural man — and identifies it instead as the cross of Christ, the doctrine of salvation by a crucified Christ, of peace and reconciliation by the blood of his cross, and of righteousness, pardon, atonement and satisfaction by the offering up of himself as a sacrifice for sin. On the quotation he gives the Hebrew as read in the English version and the Septuagint rendering which the apostle substantially follows, and takes the sense of the prophecy to be that in the times of the Messiah, under the gospel dispensation, the mysteries of grace should be hid from the wise rabbins among the Jews, the Scribes and Pharisees, for all their sagacity, parts and learning. Calvin reads the first clause as a concession deliberately made: since it might very readily be objected that the gospel is commonly held in contempt if presented in so bare and abject a form, Paul concedes this of his own accord, but by adding that it is so only in the estimation of those who perish he intimates that no regard must be paid to their judgment — for who would choose to despise the gospel at the expense of perishing? The statement must therefore be understood as allowing that the preaching of the cross has nothing of human wisdom to recommend it to esteem, while the wisdom of God shines forth in it notwithstanding, and he indirectly reproves their perverted judgement. From the prophet he shows further how unreasonable it is that the truth of the gospel should be regarded with prejudice on the ground that the wise of this world hold it in contempt, not to say derision, since it is evident from the words that their opinion is reckoned as nothing in the account of God; the passage threatens that the Lord will avenge himself upon the hypocrisy of the people by this kind of punishment, and its application here is that the thing is nothing new.

Clarke renders the phrase as the doctrine of or concerning the cross, that is, the doctrine which proclaims salvation to a lost world through the crucifixion of Christ, and holds that properly speaking there are but two classes of men known where the gospel is preached — the unbelievers and gainsayers, who are perishing, and the obedient believers, who are in a state of salvation — so that to those who continue in the first state the preaching of salvation through the merit of a crucified Saviour is folly, while to those who believe it is the power of God. On the prophecy he takes the wise to be the philosophers, who in their investigations seek nothing less than God and whose highest discoveries amount to nothing in comparison of the grand truths concerning God, the invisible world and the true end of man which the gospel has brought to light; and he adds that the discoveries which are really useful have been made by men who feared God and conscientiously credited divine revelation, naming Newton, Boyle and Pascal among many others, against the sceptics. Wesley glosses the perishing as those who perish by obstinately rejecting the only name whereby they can be saved, and the saved as those now saved from their sins and in the way to everlasting salvation, for whom the word is the great instrument of the power of God; the quotation he calls remarkably applicable to this great event.

Barnes renders the phrase as the word or doctrine of the cross, which proclaims salvation only through the atonement made on the cross, and argues that it cannot mean the bare statement that Christ died as a martyr on a cross, since if that were all there would be nothing contemptible in it — the statement that Polycarp or Ignatius or Cranmer died as martyrs does not appear foolish but is a historical truth whose subjects excite high admiration — so that what offends must be the doctrine of atonement itself. On the quotation he sets the Hebrew as rendered in the English version beside the Septuagint version which corresponds substantially with the apostle’s citation, judges that the sense in the Hebrew is not materially different, and explains the original meaning from the iniquity and stupidity of Jerusalem. Ellicott observes that in the original the contrast comes out more strongly than in English, the same phrase being repeated so that the word of the cross stands against the wisdom of mere words above, and that this is the word of real power; he prefers the continuous participles, those that are perishing and us who are being saved, the former referring to those who have not received the gospel and the latter to those who have, and calls the cross and all it represents the greatest display of the power of God. The quotation he notes consists of two passages in Isaiah taken from the Greek version with one word altered, bringing to nothing standing where the older text conceals, and remarks that words which originally applied to those who assumed to be the guides of the Jewish race apply with greater force to those who would presume to be Christian leaders. Robertson reads the phrase literally as the preaching, that of the cross, set opposite the wisdom of word in the previous verse, and observes that through this incidental allusion to preaching the apostle passes to a new subject, the discussions in the Corinthian church being for a time forgotten while he takes the opportunity of correcting his converts for their undue exaltation of human eloquence and wisdom. The dative he calls one of disadvantage and the present participle timeless, of those in the path to destruction, which he is careful to say is not annihilation. The quotation he traces to the failure of worldly statesmanship in the presence of the Assyrian invasion, applied by Paul to his argument with force: the wisdom of the wise is often folly and the understanding of the understanding often rejected, there is such a thing as the ignorance of the learned and the wisdom of the simple-minded, and God’s wisdom rises in the Cross sheer above a human philosophizing which is still scoffing at it.

Chrysostom explains the contempt by an image from the sickroom: to the sick and gasping even wholesome meats are unpleasant and friends and relations burdensome, often not even recognized but rather accounted intruders, and much like this is the case of those perishing in their souls, who do not know the things that tend to salvation and consider those who are careful about them to be troublesome. This ensues not from the nature of the thing, he insists, but from their disease; and just as the insane hate those who take care of them and revile them besides, so it is with unbelievers — and as those insulted by the insane then more than ever compassionate them and weep, so should it be here. Cyril of Jerusalem exhorts that we not be ashamed of the Cross of our Saviour but rather glory in it, since the word of the Cross is a stumbling-block to Jews and foolishness to Gentiles but to us salvation; it was not a mere man who died for us but the Son of God, God made man. He argues from the Passover: if the lamb under Moses drove the destroyer far away, did not much rather the Lamb of God, which takes away the sin of the world, deliver us from our sins — the blood of a silly sheep gave salvation, and shall not the Blood of the Only-begotten much rather save?

debates: What the preaching of the cross denotes: Gill first rules out the Christian’s own cross and keeps it to the cross of Christ, while Barnes argues from the reception of other martyrdoms — which excite admiration rather than contempt — that the offence cannot lie in the bare fact of a martyr’s death but only in the doctrine of atonement.

How the two classes are described: Clarke treats them as two fixed classes of men, the gainsayers and the obedient believers; Ellicott and Robertson insist on the continuous participles, those who are perishing and those who are being saved, Robertson adding that the destruction meant is not annihilation; Wesley locates the perishing in an obstinate rejection of the name.
outliers: Chrysostom accounts for the contempt of the gospel by disease rather than judgement, comparing unbelievers to the insane who revile the very people nursing them, and concluding that they are to be wept over rather than resented.

Clarke answers the charge that faith hinders learning with a roster of believing natural philosophers — Newton, Boyle, Pascal — claiming the genuinely useful discoveries for men who credited revelation.
Cyril of Jerusalem argues the value of the Cross a fortiori from the Passover, setting the blood of a silly sheep that saved Israel against the Blood of the Only-begotten.
Ellicott observes that the citation is not one text but two passages of Isaiah joined, following the Greek version with a single word altered.

20.pericope_label: Where is the wise? where is the scribe? where is the disputer of this world? hath not God made foolish the wisdom of this world? For after that in the wisdom of God the world by wisdom knew not God, it pleased God by the foolishness of preaching to save them that believe

schools.summary: Gill holds that these are the apostle’s own words, though he may allude to a place where there are some phrases much like them whose meaning is very different, and notes that the Talmudists interpret those phrases in a sense pretty near the apostle’s. On the wisdom of God he canvasses three referents: Christ, who is the wisdom of God and was in the world though the world of the Jews and their chief rabbins with all their wisdom knew neither him nor his Father; the gospel, which is also so called, and which came into both the Jewish and the Gentile world without either knowing by their natural wisdom the God of grace revealed in it; or rather the works of creation, in which there is a visible display of the wisdom of God — and yet the world by wisdom knew not God. Calvin denies outright that the triumphant question is drawn from the prophet: Paul has not taken this sentiment from Isaiah, as is commonly thought, but speaks in his own person, since the passage which interpreters point to has nothing corresponding to the subject in hand or nearly approaching it, promising as it does deliverance from the yoke of Sennacherib and describing the misery of those oppressed by foreign tyranny. On the failure of natural knowledge he sets out the right order of things, that man, contemplating the wisdom of God in his works by the light of the understanding furnished him by nature, might arrive at an acquaintance with him; since that order has been reversed through man’s depravity, God designs in the first place to make us see ourselves to be fools, and secondly, as a token of his wisdom, presents to us what has some appearance of folly — an inversion of the order of things which the ingratitude of mankind deserved. By the wisdom of God in that clause he means the workmanship of the whole world, which is an illustrious token and clear manifestation of it.

John Lightfoot supplies from the rabbis the very sequence of the three titles, a saying that God showed to Adam every generation and the disputers of it, every generation and the wise men of it, every generation and the scribes of it, every generation and the governors of it, noting that the words are recited with some variation elsewhere; the first term he glosses as a wise man who taught others, the second as a scribe, that is any learned man as distinguished from the common people and especially a Father of the tradition. On the wisdom of God he argues that the phrase is not to be understood of that wisdom which had God for its author but of that which had God for its object, and is to be rendered wisdom about God: among the heathen there was a wisdom about natural things and a wisdom about God, that is, divinity, so that the sense is that the world in its divinity could not by its wisdom know God.

Clarke holds that these words most manifestly refer to the Jews, since the places in Isaiah to which the apostle refers cannot be understood of any but the Jews, and maps each Greek term onto its Hebrew counterpart in the prophets: the wise man answers to the chakam, whose office it was to teach others; the scribe to the sopher, which signifies any man of learning as distinguished from the common people and especially any master of the traditions; and the disputer to the darshan, the propounder of questions and the seeker of allegorical and mystical senses. On the wisdom of God he quotes John Lightfoot by name and at length for the doctrine that the phrase means wisdom about God rather than wisdom from God, and takes the plain meaning of the verse to be that the wise men of the world, especially the Greek philosophers, who possessed every advantage human nature could have independently of divine revelation and had cultivated their minds to the uttermost, could never arrive at the knowledge of God. Wesley identifies the deliverance of Judea from Sennacherib as what the prophet refers to, and calls the apostle’s clause a bold and beautiful allusion in which he triumphs over all the opposition of human wisdom to the victorious gospel — asking what the wise men of the Gentiles, or the Jewish scribes, or the disputers of this world could do against it, those among both who, proud of their acuteness, were fond of controversy and thought they could confute all opponents. God has made that wisdom foolish, he says, by showing it to be very foolishness; and the failure he refers to God’s wise disposals in leaving them to make the trial, though the whole creation declared its Creator and he declared himself by all the prophets.

Barnes notes that language similar to this occurs in Isaiah, and states the principle by which the apostle uses it: without designing to quote the words as having an original reference to the subject now under consideration, Paul uses them as any man does language with which he or his readers are familiar and which will convey his meaning, since a man familiar with the Bible will naturally make use of Scripture expressions in conveying his ideas; in the prophet the passage refers to the deliverance of the people from the threatened invasion of Sennacherib.
