On the following clause he says the phrase is susceptible of two interpretations, the first making it refer to the wisdom of God evinced in the works of creation and the demonstration of his existence and attributes found there, so that the apostle means the world by a survey of the works of God did not know him but remained, notwithstanding those works, in deep darkness; and he holds that after all the experience of the world it was ascertained that men would never by their own wisdom come to the true knowledge of God, so that it pleased him to devise another plan for salvation. Ellicott takes the second quotation, originally a song of triumph over the enemies of Israel, to be given a general application; the first title he refers generally to those who would exalt human knowledge, the second to the Jew and the third to the Greek who discussed philosophy, and insists that the qualifying phrase governs all three and not exclusively the last, the word meaning not the physical world but, in an ethical sense, this age in contrast to that which is to come. The clause about God’s wisdom he says can scarcely be taken as expressing a kind of approval of God’s wisdom in so arranging the method of revelation, but rather as referring to the wisdom evidenced in nature and in the teachings of lawgivers and prophets, the world by its own wisdom failing to attain a knowledge of God in the wisdom displayed in creation. Robertson says Paul makes use of the prophet without exact quotation, identifies the setting as the sudden retreat of Sennacherib with the annihilation of his officers, and cites the observation that a surprisingly exact picture of the scene survives on an Assyrian tablet in the British Museum; he notes the absence of the article in each of the rhetorical questions though the idea is clearly definite, and refers the first title probably to the Greek philosopher and the second to the Jewish scribe. The two wisdoms he sets in contrast, calls the verb an effective aorist and the clause a solemn dirge of doom on both Greek philosophy and Jewish theology that failed to know God, and asks whether modern philosophy has done better, remarking that there is today even a godless theology. On the last phrase he presses that the noun is not the act of heralding but the message proclaimed, so that proclamation is the better rendering.

debates: Whether the triple question quotes Isaiah: Calvin denies it outright and holds that Paul speaks in his own person, since the passage usually cited has nothing to do with the subject; Gill and Barnes allow familiar prophetic language used without any intention of quotation; Ellicott and Robertson treat it as a quotation loosely made and given a general application.

Whether the three titles are all Jewish: Clarke says they most manifestly refer to the Jews and maps each onto a Hebrew office from the prophets, while Ellicott and Robertson divide them by nation, the scribe standing for the Jew and the disputer for the Greek.

What the wisdom of God means in the second verse: John Lightfoot, followed by Clarke, makes it wisdom about God — the heathen’s divinity as distinguished from their natural philosophy — while Barnes, Ellicott and Calvin all refer it to God’s own wisdom displayed in creation, and Gill canvasses Christ and the gospel before preferring creation.
outliers: Robertson breaks off from the exegesis to ask whether modern philosophy has done any better than the ancient, and observes that there is now even a godless theology.

Calvin explains the failure as a deliberate inversion: the natural order was that man should climb from the works to their Maker, and because depravity overturned it God now begins by convincing us we are fools and then offers something wearing the appearance of folly.
Clarke reproduces John Lightfoot’s note on the wisdom of God verbatim and under his name — the third borrowing from him in this chapter.
Robertson insists the word rendered preaching means the message proclaimed and not the act of heralding, so that what is called foolishness is the content rather than the performance.

22.pericope_label: For the Jews require a sign, and the Greeks seek after wisdom: but we preach Christ crucified, unto the Jews a stumblingblock, and unto the Greeks foolishness; but unto them which are called, both Jews and Greeks, Christ the power of God, and the wisdom of God. Because the foolishness of God is wiser than men; and the weakness of God is stronger than men

schools.summary: Gill explains the demand for a sign from the nation’s history, that the Jews had always been used to miracles in confirmation of the mission of the prophets sent to them and would not believe unless signs and wonders were wrought; yet though miracles were wrought in great numbers, and such as never man did, they remained incredulous and persisted in demanding a sign from heaven and in their own way. He notes that the apostle and his fellow ministers continued preaching the doctrine of salvation by a crucified Christ, and him only, regardless of the sentiments and opinions of Jews and Gentiles and in opposition to all their cavils. The called he takes as those effectually called by the grace of God, not merely externally but internally, who, being called out of darkness and savingly illuminated by the Spirit, see wisdom, beauty, glory, excellency and suitableness in Christ and in his gospel, having felt the power of it upon their souls. On the last verse he insists there is no such thing as foolishness in God nor the least degree of weakness in him, the apostle meaning by an ironical concession that which the men of the world esteem so; by it he understands Christ, who as crucified is counted foolishness yet is wiser than men, greater in wisdom even than Solomon, having all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge in him. Calvin takes the verse as explanatory of what precedes but observes that the apostle does not simply explain, going a step farther by saying that the Jews do not merely despise the gospel but abhor it: the Jews desire through miracles to have an evidence of divine power before their eyes, while the Greeks are fond of what gratifies human intellect by the applause of acuteness. The contrast of the called he uses to show that the unfavourable reception of Christ was owing neither to any fault on his part nor to the natural disposition of mankind generally, but arose from the depravity of those who were not enlightened by God, inasmuch as the elect of God, whether Jews or Gentiles, are hindered by nothing from coming to Christ and finding in him a sure salvation. On the closing comparison he says that while the Lord deals with us in such a way as to seem to act foolishly, because he does not exhibit his wisdom, what so appears surpasses all the ingenuity of men, and while he appears to act with weakness in consequence of concealing his power, that weakness as it is reckoned is stronger than any power of men; but we must always keep in view that there is a concession here, since no one can but perceive that in strict propriety neither foolishness nor weakness can be ascribed to God.

Clarke records that instead of the singular a great many manuscripts, versions and fathers read the plural, signs, a reading he calls undoubtedly genuine and which has been admitted into the text, and remarks that there never was a people in the universe more difficult to be persuaded of the truth than the Jews, who would never have received their religion had it not been proved by the most striking and indubitable miracles. The offence of the crucified Messiah he explains from the manner of the coming: Jesus came meek, lowly and impoverished, not seeking worldly glory nor affecting worldly pomp, whereas they expected the Messiah to come as a mighty prince and conqueror, and because he did not come so they were offended at him. The called he takes as those, both of Jews and Greeks, who were by the preaching of the gospel called or invited to the marriage feast and have accordingly believed, and who prove the doctrine divinely powerful to enlighten and convert the soul and a proof of God’s infinite wisdom, which has found out such an effectual way to glorify both his justice and his mercy. On the last verse he holds that the things of God’s appointment which seem to men foolishness are infinitely beyond the highest degree of human wisdom, and that those works of God which appear to superficial observers weak and contemptible surpass all the efforts of human power, the means appointed for salvation being so wisely imagined and so energetically powerful that all who properly use them shall infallibly be brought to the end. Wesley glosses the first demand as more signs still, after all they have seen already, and the second as the depths of philosophy and the charms of eloquence; the preaching he describes as plain and historical rather than rhetorical or philosophical, and sets its two receptions exactly opposite the two demands — a stumbling-block just opposite to the signs demanded, and a silly tale just opposite to the wisdom sought. The called he glosses as those who obey the heavenly calling and who experience first that Christ is the power and then that he is the wisdom of God, receiving him with his cross, his death, his life and his kingdom; and the closing verse as meaning that the gospel scheme, which the world judges mere foolishness, is wiser than the wisdom of men, and, weak as they account it, stronger than all their strength.

Barnes describes the demand for a sign as characteristic of that people, since God had manifested himself to them by miracles and wonders in a remarkable manner in past times, so that they greatly prided themselves on the fact and always demanded a miracle of any new messenger professing to be sent from God, a propensity they often evinced with the Lord Jesus himself. Against the Jew and the Greek he sets the Christian preachers, who make the crucified Christ the grand subject of their instructions and glory only in the cross; the emphasis, he says, falls on the word crucified, since the Jews would have made the Messiah they expected no less an object of glorifying than the apostles did, but spurned the doctrine of a crucified one. The called he takes as all true Christians, whether originally of Jewish or Gentile extraction, who have a common view of the crucified Saviour and see the plan to be wise. On the last verse he warns that the passage is not to be understood as affirming that what God appoints is really foolish or unwise, but that it appears so to men, and suggests the apostle may refer to those parts of the divine administration where the wisdom of the plan is not seen or the reason of what God does is concealed; what is so called is better adapted to accomplish important ends, and more certainly effectual, than the schemes of men. Ellicott notes that the Greek has no article with either name, so that the reference is not to the Jews and the Gentiles as nations but to Jewish-minded persons who desired visible portents to support the teaching and to those of Greek taste who desired an actual and clear philosophic proof of it, and holds that the gospel of Christ crucified made its way by those very qualities which they regarded as weakness and folly, vindicating itself as a power mightier than any sign a Jew might ask and a wisdom surpassing any merely intellectual wisdom a Greek might desire. Of the called he remarks that Paul always speaks of all Christians by that name and never uses the word in the narrower sense to which some modern religious sects have restricted it. On the closing comparison he insists that the sense is not wiser than the wisdom of men, as some understand the passage, but wiser than men themselves, the word embracing all that men can know or hope ever to know, and correspondingly that the weakness of God is stronger than men. Robertson takes the construction as a protasis answered by the two following verses, cites the antithesis that the Jews claimed to have the truth while the Greeks were seekers, and glosses the main verb as proclaiming rather than discussing or disputing, its object being Christ as crucified, neither a sign-shower nor a philosopher. The word for the stumbling-block he illustrates from the papyri as a trap or snare, which here tripped the Jews who wanted a conquering Messiah; the crucified Christ he calls God’s answer to both Jew and Greek, understood by those with open minds. On the last verse he takes the neuter singulars as abstract — the foolish act of God, the weak act of God as men think — and calls the construction a condensed comparison, wiser than the wisdom of men, a common Greek idiom and quite forcible, which brushes all men aside; the Cross, he adds, seemed God’s defeat.

debates: Who the called are: Gill takes them as those effectually called inwardly and not merely externally, and Calvin makes the whole difference elective, tracing the rejection to a depravity from which the elect alone are exempt; Clarke reads the word as invitation accepted; Ellicott warns expressly that the apostle applies it to all Christians and never in the narrower sense to which some modern sects have restricted it.

What the closing comparison is with: Ellicott insists the sense is not wiser than the wisdom of men, as some understand the passage, but wiser than men themselves and all they could ever know, while Robertson gives precisely that rejected reading, calling it a condensed comparison and a common Greek idiom.
outliers: Clarke supports a plural reading of the word for sign, calling it undoubtedly genuine and noting it has been admitted into the printed text.

Robertson finds in the papyri that the word rendered stumbling-block means a trap or a snare, and applies it to Jews who were tripped by expecting a conquering Messiah; of the second half of the last verse he remarks that the Cross seemed God’s defeat.

Gill, Barnes and Calvin all stop to insist that the foolishness and weakness named here are a concession to how men speak and not predicates of God, none of them willing to let the phrase stand unqualified.

26.pericope_label: For ye see your calling, brethren, how that not many wise men after the flesh, not many mighty, not many noble, are called: but God hath chosen the foolish things of the world to confound the wise; and God hath chosen the weak things of the world to confound the things which are mighty; and base things of the world, and things which are despised, hath God chosen, yea, and things which are not, to bring to nought things that are: that no flesh should glory in his presence

schools.summary: Gill takes calling to designate the men called by grace, as circumcision and uncircumcision stand for circumcised and uncircumcised persons and election for elect persons, and says the manner of their calling and what sort of persons they were is what they did or might or ought to observe. Of the foolish things he notes that the Jews themselves, in distinction from their wise rabbins and doctors, called others the fools of the world, and that those whom God chose from all eternity, as appears by his calling them in time, are such as with respect to the wisdom of the world are foolish, lacking the sagacity, penetration, knowledge and learning that many others have, and therefore esteemed foolish. The base things he glosses as those reckoned the filth of the world and the offscouring of all things, men of mean birth, education and business of life. The closing purpose he expounds by listing what is excluded: men may not glory in their blood, birth, families, lineage and natural descent, nor in their might, power and dominion, nor in their riches, wealth and substance, nor in their wisdom, learning and parts — for however these may be gloried in before men, they are of no account before God, who has taken a method that shuts them all out. Calvin observes that the mood of the Greek verb is doubtful and that the indicative suits the context equally as well as the imperative, so that he leaves it to the reader’s choice which to prefer, the meaning being manifestly the same in either case: on the indicative the apostle summons them as witnesses of a thing that is manifest and calls them forward to a thing present, while on the imperative he stirs them up. Of the things which are not he notes that similar terms are used in Romans but in a different sense, for there, describing the universal call of the pious, the apostle says we are nothing previously to being called, which must be understood as referring to reality in the sight of God however we may appear to be something in the eyes of men, whereas here the nothingness spoken of must be viewed as referring to the opinion of men. On the last clause he says that though the term denotes all mankind, here it carries a particular idea, the Spirit beating down their pride by speaking of mankind in terms of contempt; it is a sentiment worthy to be kept in remembrance that there is nothing left us in which we may justly glory, since many delight themselves for the moment in a false glorying which quickly vanishes like smoke.

Henry observes that God did not choose philosophers, nor orators, nor statesmen, nor men of wealth and power and interest in the world, to publish the gospel of grace and peace, since he best judges what men and what measures serve the purposes of his glory. He is careful, however, not to turn the statement into an absolute one: though not many noble are usually called by divine grace, there have been some such in every age who have not been ashamed of the gospel of Christ, and persons of every rank stand in need of pardoning grace; often a humble Christian, poor as to this world, has more true knowledge than the learned.

Clarke takes the calling to be the state of grace and blessedness to which they are invited, and thinks the verb should be read in the imperative — take heed to, or consider, your calling — noting that the word men is not in the original and that Paul seems to allude to the Corinthian believers in particular, in opposition to the high and worldly notions of the Jews. Of the choosing he says God has chosen by means of men esteemed rude and illiterate to confound the greatest of the Greek philosophers and overturn their systems, and by means of men weak and without secular power to confound the scribes and Pharisees and spread the doctrine of Christ crucified over all the land of Judea in spite of the sanhedrin. The base and despised things he identifies with the Gentiles and the Gentile converts, considered base and despicable in the eyes of the Jews, who counted them no better than dogs and repeatedly called them the things that are not; by these very people, converted to Christianity, God brought to nought all the Jewish pretensions and annihilated the whole Jewish polity. The closing purpose he explains by saying that God does his mighty works in such a way as proves that, though he may condescend to employ men as instruments, they have no part either in the contrivance or in the energy by which such works are performed. Wesley glosses the wise after the flesh as wise in the account of the world and the mighty as men of power and authority, and notes that the Jews frequently called the Gentiles them that are not, in such supreme contempt did they hold them, while the things that are stand for those in high esteem. The word flesh he calls a fit appellation, since flesh is fair but withering as grass, and adds that in God we ought to glory.

Barnes takes the design to be to show that the gospel did not depend for its success on human wisdom, since those blessed by it had not generally been drawn from the elevated ranks of life but from humble life, God showing his power by choosing the ignorant and the abased. To confound he glosses as to bring to shame, that is, to humble the wise by showing how little God regarded their wisdom; the base things he renders literally as those not of noble or illustrious birth, and the despised as those the world regards as objects of contempt. Of the connective inserted before the last member he complains that it does nothing to illustrate the sense but rather enfeebles it, the language being a striking instance of Paul’s manner of expressing himself with great strength. The final clause he explains as meaning that no men, no class of men, should boast, the word flesh being often used to denote men, and that man should really have nothing of which to boast, the whole scheme being adapted to humble and subdue him. Ellicott prefers the imperative, see your calling, and takes the apostle to be directing them to the facts of their own calling as an illustration of what he has just written — that though there were perhaps a few of high birth and education who were called and responded, these are not many; he quotes the remark that the ancient Christians were for the greater part slaves. The neuter of the foolish things he takes to be used probably for the purpose of generalising, expressing the qualities of the men whom God has chosen, while the masculine of the wise shows that it is still of persons the apostle speaks. Of the last member he says the climax loses somewhat of its force by the insertion of a connective which is not in some of the best manuscripts and of another word which is in no manuscript at all: omitting the first, the sentence is not an addition to the things already mentioned but a general and emphatic summary of all that has been contrasted with its opposites, with a slight pause before it. Robertson notes that the opening form serves equally for the imperative present active plural and the indicative, and that either makes sense; the calling he defines as the act of calling by God, based not on the external condition of those called but on God’s sovereign love, and a clinching illustration of the argument. The verb of choosing he parses as first aorist middle, to pick out for oneself, expanding the idea of the calling, and observes that it occurs three times with the purpose stated each time — twice that God might put to shame and once that he might bring to naught, that is, make idle — with a further purpose added for variety which appeals to God’s ultimate choice in all three instances; the aorist middle of the verb for boasting brings out sharply that not a single boast is to be made, and the preposition, common in the papyri, means in the eye of God.

Chrysostom sums up the argument to this point: having said that the foolishness of God is wiser than men, the apostle has shown that human wisdom is cast out both by the testimony of the Scriptures and by the issue of events — by the testimony where he says he will destroy the wisdom of the wise, and by the event where he puts his argument in the form of a question, asking where the wise is and where the scribe. At the same time, Chrysostom adds, he proved that the thing is not new but ancient, since it was presignified and foretold from the beginning, which is why he says it is written.

debates: Whether the opening verb is indicative or imperative: Ellicott and Clarke both read it as a command to look at their own calling; Robertson observes that the form is identical for either and that both make sense; Calvin declines to decide, leaving the choice to the reader on the ground that the meaning is the same either way.

What the last member of the series means and whether its connectives belong: Ellicott finds one absent from the best manuscripts and another in no manuscript at all, so that the phrase summarises rather than adds, and Barnes says the inserted word enfeebles the sense; Clarke and Wesley identify the phrase as a Jewish term of contempt for the Gentiles; Calvin distinguishes this nothingness, which exists only in the opinion of men, from the nothingness he finds in Romans, which is real in the sight of God.
outliers: Henry refuses to let the statement harden into an absolute one, insisting that not many noble is not none, that some in every age have not been ashamed of the gospel, and that persons of every rank need pardoning grace alike.
Calvin openly leaves a grammatical decision to the reader rather than settling it, holding that nothing in the sense depends on it.
Clarke reads the whole passage as aimed at Jewish pretensions, making the despised Gentile converts the very instrument by which the Jewish polity was annihilated.

30.pericope_label: But of him are ye in Christ Jesus, who of God is made unto us wisdom, and righteousness, and sanctification, and redemption: that, according as it is written, He that glorieth, let him glory in the Lord

schools.summary: Gill takes the words to direct to the proper object of glorying and to show the high honour the called are brought to in Christ, set against their outward meanness, folly, weakness, poverty and contempt. They are first of God the Father, of his own rich free grace and goodness, without any regard to motive, merit or desert of theirs, put into Christ by electing grace, in whom they are preserved and blessed — which he calls their original secret being in him — and this is made manifest by regenerating grace in their being made new creatures, which likewise is not owing to blood, nor to the will of the flesh, nor to the will of man. Calvin explains that the apostle now shows the application of all this to them, the words being emphatic as though he had said that they have their beginning from God, who calls the things that are not while passing by those that appear to be, and that their subsistence is founded upon Christ, so that they have no occasion to be proud; nor is it of creation merely that he speaks, but of that spiritual existence into which we are born again by the grace of God, against the many who, while not avowedly inclined to draw back from God, nevertheless seek something apart from Christ as if he alone did not suffice. On the closing clause he marks the end God has in view in bestowing all things upon us in Christ — that we may not claim any merit to ourselves but may give him all the praise; for God does not despoil us with the view of leaving us bare, but forthwith clothes us with his glory, yet on this condition, that whenever we would glory we must go out of ourselves. In short, man, brought to nothing in his own estimation and acknowledging that there is nothing good anywhere but in God alone, must renounce all desire for his own glory and with all his might aspire and aim at the glory of God exclusively.

Clarke observes that even the good they possess is granted by God, since it is by and through him that Christ Jesus comes and with him all the blessings of the gospel dispensation. He defines each title against a rival: the wisdom is that evangelical wisdom which far excels the wisdom of the philosopher and the scribe and even that legal constitution which is called the wisdom of the Jews; the righteousness is justification, procuring for us that remission of sins which the law could not give; and the sanctification procures for and works in us not merely an external and relative holiness, as was that of the Jews, but a real one. On the closing quotation he sets out the prophet’s words in full — that the wise man not glory in his wisdom, nor the mighty man in his might, nor the rich man in his riches, but that he who glories glory in this, that he understands and knows the Lord who exercises loving-kindness, judgment and righteousness in the earth — and draws the rule that since all good is of and from God, whoever has wisdom, strength, riches, pardon, holiness or any other blessing, temporal or spiritual, should acknowledge that he has nothing but what he has received. Wesley glosses the opening as out of God’s free grace and mercy and the state as being engrafted into Christ Jesus, and defines each title against the condition it replaces: wisdom for those who were before utterly foolish and ignorant, righteousness as the sole ground of our justification for those who were before under the wrath and curse of God, sanctification as a principle of universal holiness for those who were before altogether dead in sin, and redemption as complete deliverance from all evil and eternal bliss both of soul and body. The final clause he states negatively — glory not in himself, not in the flesh, not in the world.

Barnes says the sense is that it is by God’s agency and power, not by philosophy nor from ourselves but by his mercy, and places the emphasis of the verse on the two words declaring what they are: they are Christians not by the agency of man but by the agency of God, owing their hopes to him, and the apostle keeps prominently in view that it was not of their philosophy, wealth or rank that they were raised to these privileges. The quotation he identifies as made from Jeremiah, not literally, the apostle having condensed the sense of the prophet into a few words while retaining essentially his idea, and glossing to glory in the Lord as not ascribing one’s salvation to human abilities, learning or rank but entirely to God. From this he draws that the design of the plan of salvation is to exalt God in view of the mind and to make us humble, which is the design also of all his works, since all just views of the creation tend to produce true humility. Ellicott states the consequence — so far from boasting in his presence, we all owe all to him, he being the author of the spiritual life of those in union with Christ — and presses the tense, who was made and not is made, the past referring back to the fact of the Incarnation, in which Christ became to us God’s revelation of himself and so gave us a wisdom from the source of all wisdom which utterly surpasses any we could have derived from nature or from man; not only is Christ the source of whatever true wisdom we have, he adds, but also of whatever righteousness and holiness, and beyond all that he is our redemption. The quotation he calls not literal but an adaptation and paraphrase of the Greek version, and takes our only true boasting before God to be that we are in Christ and owe all to him, quoting the ancient remark that the apostle always fastens his readers on with nails to the name of Christ; with this, he notes, the general explanation of God’s method concludes, before the apostle turns to his own conduct. Robertson reads the opening preposition as out of God, who chose them, the choice having been made in the sphere of Christ Jesus, and this being God’s wisdom; he stresses that the verb is became rather than was, pointing to the Incarnation, Cross and Resurrection, and argues from the arrangement of the connectives that the three following nouns are an explanation of the first rather than co-ordinate additions to it. On the last verse he supposes a probable ellipse of the kind common in these letters, notes that some explain the imperative as a broken construction instead, and calls the quotation shortened; he closes by citing the judgement that these verses, for what they show of the origin of Paul’s congregations among the lower classes in the large towns, are one of the most important historical witnesses to primitive Christianity.

debates: Whether the three titles following wisdom are co-ordinate with it or explanatory of it: Robertson argues from the pattern of connectives that they are an epexegesis of the first, while Ellicott presents them as successive additions — not only wisdom but righteousness and holiness, and beyond all that redemption — and Clarke and Wesley expound all four as distinct benefits.

How loosely the closing quotation is made: Barnes calls it a condensation of the prophet’s sense retaining his idea, Ellicott an adaptation and paraphrase rather than a citation, and Robertson a shortened quotation requiring an ellipse to be supplied, noting that others account for the grammar by treating the imperative as a broken construction.
outliers: Calvin denies that the stripping is an end in itself: God does not despoil us with the view of leaving us bare but immediately clothes us with his own glory, on the single condition that when we glory we go outside ourselves to do it.

Robertson ends on the paragraph’s value as evidence rather than doctrine, citing the judgement that what it shows about the social origin of Paul’s congregations in the large towns makes it one of the most important historical witnesses to primitive Christianity.
